CausalChain: Chronic alcohol intake -> enhanced alcohol metabolism (ADH/CYP2E1) -> generation of acetaldehyde and ROS -> liver injury/fibrosis; Concurrently, alcohol disrupts gut microbiota composition -> increased intestinal permeability -> endotoxins (LPS) translocate to liver -> activation of Kupffer cells -> release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α) -> in individuals with PNPLA3 risk alleles, impaired lipid handling further amplifies oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling -> epigenetic modifications in hepatic cells -> enhanced oncogenic transformation leading to HCC
Hypothesis: In patients with alcohol-associated liver disease, the presence of PNPLA3 risk variants synergistically amplifies the pro-inflammatory and fibrogenic effects induced by alcohol-mediated gut dysbiosis and endotoxin translocation, thereby promoting epigenetic reprogramming of hepatic cells that drives hepatocarcinogenesis. Targeting the gut–liver axis may thus be an effective strategy to reduce HCC risk in genetically predisposed individuals.
Abstract: We propose that in patients with alcohol‐associated liver disease, there exists a “double hit” where chronic alcohol consumption not only induces hepatocyte injury directly via its metabolism to reactive oxygen species and acetaldehyde, but also disrupts the gut microbiome, leading to increased intestinal permeability and subsequent endotoxin (LPS) translocation. In individuals harboring genetic risk factors such as the PNPLA3 variant, the pro‐inflammatory cascade (mediated by Kupffer cell activation and IL-6/STAT3 signaling) is further potentiated. This combined sequence of events may induce epigenetic and fibrogenic changes in hepatic cells, thereby increasing the risk of transformation into hepatocellular carcinoma. Interventions that modulate the gut microbiota or block specific inflammatory pathways may therefore have potential to mitigate HCC risk in genetically predisposed populations.
